paragraphs: The captain had slid back into his old tone of bitter clowning. Still, Alyosha sensed that the man trusted him. Had anyone else been standing there in Alyosha’s place, he thought, the captain would never have spoken so openly or told what he had just told. That gave Alyosha courage, though his heart was close to tears.
“Oh, I would so love to be friends with your boy!” he cried. “If you could arrange it—”
“Of course, sir,” the captain muttered.

“But now hear something quite different!” Alyosha went on. “I have a message for you. My brother Dmitri has wronged his fiancée too. She is a noble-hearted girl, and you have probably heard of her. I have every right to tell you how she was wronged. In fact I ought to, because the moment she heard of the insult to you, and of your unfortunate situation, she sent me to bring you this help. That was just now. It comes from her alone. It does not come from Dmitri, who has abandoned her, or from me, his brother, or from anyone else. It is from her, only from her! She begs you to accept it.... The same man has insulted you both. She thought of you just after he had done something similar to her, similar in its cruelty, I mean. She comes as a sister to help a brother in trouble.... She told me to persuade you to take these two hundred roubles from her, as from a sister, because she knows how badly you need them. Nobody will know about it, and no one can start any unjust gossip. Here are the two hundred roubles. I swear you must take them, unless—unless all men on earth are meant to be enemies! But there are brothers even on earth.... Your heart is generous ... you must see that, you must,” and Alyosha held out two new hundred-rouble notes, the rainbow-colored kind.

The two of them stood by the great stone near the fence, and nobody was close by. The notes seemed to hit the captain with tremendous force. He started, but at first only out of astonishment. He had never imagined their talk would end like this. Help from anyone was the furthest thing from his dreams, let alone a sum like that!
He took the notes. For a minute he could hardly answer, and a completely new look came over his face.
“That’s for me? All that money, two hundred roubles! Good heavens! Why, I haven’t laid eyes on so much money for four years! Mercy on us! And she says she’s a sister.... Is that really true?”
“I swear that all I’ve told you is true,” cried Alyosha.
The captain went red in the face.

“Listen, my dear, listen. If I take it, I’m not behaving like a scoundrel? To you, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I won’t seem a scoundrel? No, Alexey Fyodorovitch, listen, listen,” he hurried on, plucking at Alyosha with both hands. “You’re talking me into taking it, saying it comes from a sister, but deep down in your heart, won’t you despise me if I take it, eh?”
“No, no! I swear on my salvation I won’t! And nobody will ever know except me, you, her, and one other lady, her great friend.”

“Forget the lady! Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch, at a moment like this you have to listen, because you can’t understand what these two hundred roubles mean to me now.” The poor man was working himself up, little by little, into a rambling, almost wild excitement. He had lost his balance, and he talked very fast, as if afraid he would be cut off before he could say everything.

“Never mind that it’s honestly come by, from a ‘sister’ I respect and revere so highly. Do you know, I can now look after mamma and Nina, my hunchback angel of a daughter? Doctor Herzenstube came to see us, out of the goodness of his heart, and spent a whole hour examining the two of them. ‘I can’t make anything of it,’ he said. But he prescribed a mineral water, sold at the chemist’s here. He said it would surely do her good, and he ordered baths as well, with some medicine in the water. The mineral water costs thirty kopecks a bottle, and she might need forty of them. So I took the prescription, put it on the shelf under the ikons, and there it lies. And for Nina he ordered hot baths, with something dissolved in them, morning and evening. But how are we to manage a cure like that in our mansion? We have no servants, no help, no bath, not even any water! Nina has rheumatism all over, I don’t think I mentioned that. At night her whole right side aches. She’s in agony, and would you believe it, the angel suffers without a groan, so as not to wake us. We eat whatever we can find, and she will take only the scraps, what you’d hardly throw to a dog. ‘I don’t deserve it, I’m taking it from you, I’m a burden to you,’ that’s what her angel eyes are trying to say. We wait on her, but she hates it. ‘I’m a useless cripple, good for nothing.’ As if she didn’t deserve it, when she is what saves all of us, with her angelic sweetness! Without her, without her gentle word, it would be hell among us! She softens even Varvara. And don’t judge Varvara harshly either. She’s an angel too, and she’s been wronged too. She came to us for the summer with sixteen roubles she had saved from giving lessons, meant for her trip back to Petersburg in September, which is now. But we took her money and lived on it, so now she has nothing to go back with. Not that she could go back anyway, since she has to slave for us here. She’s like an overworked horse with all of us riding on her back. She waits on everyone, mends, washes, sweeps the floor, puts mamma to bed. And mamma is fretful and tearful and out of her mind! But now, with this money, I can hire a servant, you understand, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I can buy medicines for the dear creatures. I can send my student to Petersburg. I can buy beef and feed them properly. Good Lord, it’s a dream!”
Alyosha was overjoyed that he had given the man such happiness, and that the poor fellow had let himself be made happy.

“Wait, Alexey Fyodorovitch, wait,” the captain broke in, talking with frenzied speed, swept off by a fresh daydream. “Do you know, Ilusha and I may actually carry out our dream. We’ll buy a horse and cart, a black horse, he insists on black, and we’ll set off just as we pretended the other day. I have an old friend, a lawyer in K. province. A man I trust told me that if I came, this friend would give me a place as a clerk in his office. Who knows, maybe he would! So I’d simply put mamma and Nina in the cart, Ilusha would drive, and I’d walk, I’d walk.... Why, if I could just collect one debt that’s owed me, I might even have enough for that!”

“You would have enough!” cried Alyosha. “Katerina Ivanovna will send you as much more as you need. And I have money too, you know. Take what you want, as from a brother, from a friend, and pay it back later.... (You’ll get rich, you’ll get rich!) And you couldn’t have a better idea than moving to another province! It would save you, and especially your boy. You ought to go soon, before winter, before the cold sets in. Write to us when you get there, and we will always be brothers.... No, it’s not a dream!”

Alyosha was so happy he could have hugged him. But he glanced at the man and stopped short. The captain stood with his neck stretched out and his lips thrust forward, his face pale and frenzied. His lips kept moving, as if he were trying to get something out. No sound came, yet they went on moving. It was eerie.
“What is it?” asked Alyosha, startled.

“Alexey Fyodorovitch ... I ... you,” the captain muttered, stumbling, staring at him with a strange, wild, fixed gaze and a look of desperate resolve. At the same time something like a grin played on his lips. “I ... you, sir ... would you like me to show you a little trick I know?” he murmured suddenly, in a firm, quick whisper, his voice no longer stumbling.
“What trick?”
“A pretty one,” the captain whispered. His mouth was twisted to the left, and his left eye was squeezed shut. He kept staring at Alyosha.
“What’s the matter? What trick?” cried Alyosha, now truly alarmed.

“Why, look!” the captain suddenly squealed. All through the conversation he had been holding the two notes by one corner between thumb and forefinger. Now he showed them to Alyosha, then crushed them savagely into a ball in his right fist. “Do you see? Do you see?” he shrieked, white and furious. And suddenly he flung up his hand and hurled the crumpled notes onto the sand. “Do you see?” he shrieked again, pointing at them. “Look at that!”
And in a wild rage he started stamping on them with his heel, panting and shouting as he did it:
“There’s your money for you! There’s your money for you! There’s your money for you! There’s your money for you!”
Then he leaped back and drew himself up in front of Alyosha, and his whole figure spoke of unspeakable pride.

“Tell the people who sent you that the wisp of tow does not sell his honor,” he cried, raising his arm in the air. Then he whirled around and began to run. But he had not gone five steps when he turned all the way back and blew a kiss to Alyosha. He ran five paces more and turned for the last time. This time his face was not twisted with laughter. It was quivering with tears. In a tearful, broken, sobbing voice he cried:
“What could I say to my boy if I took money from you to pay for our shame?”

And then he ran on without looking back. Alyosha watched him go, grieved beyond words. Oh, he saw that until the very last moment the man had not known he would crush the notes and throw them away. The captain did not turn back, and Alyosha knew he would not. He would not follow or call him back, and he knew why. When the man was out of sight, Alyosha picked up the two notes. They were badly crumpled and had been ground into the sand, but they were not torn. They even rustled like new ones when Alyosha unfolded and smoothed them out. Once he had smoothed them, he folded them, put them in his pocket, and went to Katerina Ivanovna to report on how her errand had turned out.
